The hybrid method couples structured FDTD with unstructured FETD or FVTD on overlapping grids for electromagnetic scattering simulations.
The structured FDTD method is memory and time efficient but struggles with complex geometries.
Unstructured FETD and FVTD methods handle general geometries and small scale features accurately.
Overlapping grids allow multiple meshes with different numerical methods to coexist and exchange information via interpolation.
Cubic interpolation using Ferguson tensor products is used for structured quadrilateral meshes.
Side vertex interpolation with barycentric coordinates and Hermite polynomials is used for unstructured triangular meshes.
The time step is constrained by a CFL-like stability condition depending on minimum mesh spacing or element size.
Numerical examples include scattering by a PEC circular cylinder of diameter 15 wavelengths and a PEC NACA0012 aerofoil of length 2 wavelengths.
A perfectly matched layer (PML) of thickness one wavelength is used as an absorbing boundary condition.
The hybrid methods show excellent agreement with exact solutions and high-order frequency domain finite element methods.
The Cartesian mesh spacing used in examples is one-sixteenth of the wavelength.
Three layers of cells define the overlap region between structured and unstructured meshes.
The unstructured mesh cell size varies from one-sixteenth to one-thirtieth of the wavelength near complex geometry features.
The hybrid FDTD=FVTD method performs less well for TE wave scattering by the aerofoil due to weak boundary condition enforcement.
The hybrid approach allows for flexible mesh generation and accurate boundary representation, overcoming stair-casing errors.
The electric field in FVTD is located at triangle vertices, magnetic fields at dual mesh centroids.
The FETD method uses a two-step explicit Taylor-Galerkin time integration scheme with a lumped mass matrix.
Interpolation between FDTD and FETD requires time interpolation due to collocated finite element schemes.
The method uses a single global time step chosen to satisfy stability for all coupled schemes.
The hybrid approach enables fast and accurate large-scale electromagnetic scattering simulations.
